description: I am a Master's student in Digital Management at the University of Pavia (Italy) with a strong background in Sociology, Data Science, and Product Management. I have practical experience as a Data & AI Evaluation Specialist at Yandex, where I worked with large language models and SQL/BI dashboards. I am also the founder of an EdTech SaaS platform. For this hackathon, I am participating as a solo innovator.
summary: The Milan Heat Case is an interactive Earth System Trend Detective web application that transforms 24 years of NASA and ESA satellite telemetry into a five-phase spatial investigation of urban climate inequality across 6,079 census tracts in Milan, Italy. While climate data is often locked in static academic papers, our gamified tool empowers policymakers, urban planners, and citizens to actively measure a 6.87°C surface temperature gap within 300 meters, verify statistically significant warming acceleration in vulnerable neighborhoods (+0.858°C/decade vs. +0.825°C/decade, Spatial Lag p < 0.0001), and test real-world cooling interventions. By turning data exploration into a detective game, we lower the barrier to entry for complex spatial statistics while highlighting the "Invisible Majority" of vulnerable citizens missed by standard heat policies.
details:
How It Works:
Built with Python and Streamlit, the application guides users through five progressive investigation stages backed by spatial econometrics and machine learning:

  • Phase 1 (The Crime Scene): Users inspect 30m Landsat 8/9 Land Surface Temperature (LST) maps to uncover a 6.87°C micro-scale thermal contrast (peaking at 54°C) between Milan's historic center and a park just 300 meters away.
  • Phase 2 (The Time Bomb): Users analyze 10-year Landsat and 24-year MODIS time series (2000–2023) using Mann-Kendall tests and Sen's Slope estimators, discovering that seasonal heat gaps amplify from -0.15°C in Winter to +2.35°C in Summer.
  • Phase 3 (The Invisible Enemy): By toggling OpenStreetMap industrial polygons against OLS physical model residuals (> +2°C anomalies), users expose "Industrial Ovens" (logistics hubs, rail corridors) that account for 59.2% of extreme heat anomalies.
  • Phase 4 (The Hotspots): Users explore Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR) local coefficients (spanning -1.9°C to +1.8°C) and Spatial Lag Models (correcting for Moran's I = 0.74).
  • Phase 5 (The Invisible Majority): Using Bivariate LISA clustering, users identify 687 "Orange Zone" tracts (High Social Vulnerability + Moderate Heat) missed by conventional red-zone-only plans.

Key Discoveries:

  • The Physics Illusion: Impervious surfaces explain 57.5% of LST variance; social vulnerability adds 0% incremental R² over physics.
  • The Loneliness Trap: After strict Benjamini-Hochberg False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction, one-person households emerge as the strongest social predictor of heat exposure (+0.083°C per SD, p < 0.0001).
  • The Tree Ceiling: 64.3% of poor tracts are at the tree-cover saturation ceiling. Street tree planting yields +0.04°C cooling, whereas reflective Cool Roofs achieve -0.36°C.

Intended Impact (Actionable Output):
By integrating GHSL population data, we mapped exactly 571,146 residents (40.8% of Milan) living in compound risk zones. This transforms abstract satellite data into a precision public health tool. Municipalities can now:

  1. Prioritize Cool Roof subsidies over street trees in dense Q4 tracts.
  2. Enforce green buffer zones around the 253 industrial hotspots.
  3. Launch targeted "Check Your Neighbor" heat registries for isolated residents in the 687 invisible tracts.

Tools & Tech Stack:
Google Earth Engine (earthengine-api), Python, Streamlit, GeoPandas, PySAL (libpysal, esda, spreg, mgwr), Statsmodels (OLS, Spatial Lag, Quantile Regression), Scikit-Learn (Random Forest, Spatial Block Cross-Validation 5x5), PyMannKendall, SciPy, and Plotly.
